mainTopic: Leading communal prayer and the structure of the עמידה
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing an earlier discussion: אביי insists that a person may not treat prayer so casually that he speaks without focus and then simply repeats himself. A new משנה then deals with the שליח ציבור. If he makes a mistake, someone else replaces him at once, without the usual polite refusal, and starts from the ברכה where the mistake happened. The משנה adds that the leader should not answer אָמֵן after the כהנים, and should not do נשיאת כפים himself unless he is sure he will not lose his place. The גמרא explains that in an ordinary invitation to lead, a person should refuse once, hesitate the second time, and accept the third time. רב הונא and רב אסי then disagree about where to go back after a mistake in each section of the עמידה, and רב הונא is defended against רב ששת's challenge. רב יהודה teaches that personal requests belong only in the middle ברכות. Stories about רבי אליעזר show that prayer may be long or short, and רב חסדא teaches that one need not mention the name of the person one prays for. The עמוד ends with the rules of bowing in the עמידה for an ordinary person; the rules for people of higher rank continue on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Can a person treat Heaven so casually?
steps.stepSummary: The question rejects an overly casual attitude toward prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is such familiarity with Heaven possible?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers רב פפא's suggestion from the previous עמוד (that the person did not focus at first and focused later). He challenges the idea that a person can treat prayer as a casual conversation with Heaven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is rhetorical: that level of casualness is not acceptable. It prepares the sharp statement that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: can there be such a thing?

phrases.english: Can there be such casual familiarity toward Heaven?!

steps.triggerLanguage: חַבְרוּתָא כְּלַפֵּי שְׁמַיָּא מִי אִיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a discussion begun on the previous amud.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's suggestion that the person did not focus at first but focused later.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Prayer addressed to Heaven cannot be treated as though it requires no care.

steps.title: Concentration must begin at the outset
steps.stepSummary: The speaker insists that a person must focus from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he did not focus his mind from the beginning, we strike him with a blacksmith’s hammer until he focuses his mind.
steps.whatsHappening: The speaker gives an intentionally forceful response to someone who failed to concentrate at the start.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is not a new prayer procedure. The exaggerated image stresses that initial concentration matters and should not be brushed aside.

phrases.english: If he did not focus his mind from the beginning—
we strike him with a blacksmith’s hammer
until he focuses his mind.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי לָא כַּוֵּון דַּעְתֵּיהּ מֵעִיקָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the forceful consequence of the challenge in step 1.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A person must take concentration at the beginning of prayer seriously.

steps.title: An improper way to address God
steps.stepSummary: The משנה identifies one prayer formula as a path of מינות.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who says, “May the good bless You”—this is a path of heresy.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a rule about wording in prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sentence judges this specific wording. The משנה then moves to a different subject: mistakes made while leading communal prayer.

phrases.english: Mishna: One who says, “May the good bless You”—
this is a path of heresy.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ (הָאוֹמֵר: ״יְבָרְכוּךָ טוֹבִים״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה after the preceding discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The formula “יְבָרְכוּךָ טוֹבִים” is described as דַּרְכֵי מִינוּת.

steps.title: Replace a prayer leader who makes a mistake
steps.stepSummary: A replacement takes over immediately and does not refuse.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the person leading prayer makes a mistake, another takes his place and should not refuse at that moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives an immediate response to a mistake during communal prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual courtesy of initially declining does not apply here. The prayer has already been interrupted, so the replacement should step in promptly.

keyTerms.meaning: the person who leads communal prayer

phrases.english: One who leads prayer and makes a mistake—
another should take his place,
and should not refuse at that moment.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָעוֹבֵר לִפְנֵי הַתֵּיבָה וְטָעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from improper prayer wording to a mistake by the prayer leader.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A replacement takes over without refusing when the current leader makes a mistake.

steps.title: Where the replacement begins
steps.stepSummary: The replacement restarts the blessing in which the mistake occurred.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where does he begin? At the beginning of the blessing in which the first person made the mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks where the replacement resumes and answers immediately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The replacement does not start the entire prayer over. He goes back to the start of the affected blessing.

keyTerms.meaning: from the beginning of the blessing

phrases.english: From where does he begin?
From the beginning of the blessing in which this person made a mistake.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵהֵיכָן הוּא מַתְחִיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies how the replacement in step 4 continues the prayer.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He begins at the start of the blessing in which the mistake occurred.

steps.title: The prayer leader does not answer amen
steps.stepSummary: The leader avoids answering אָמֵן after the priests because it could disrupt his prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one leading prayer should not answer “amen” after the priests, because of confusion.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a precaution meant to keep the prayer leader from losing his place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Answering אָמֵן here could break his concentration on the sequence of prayer. The concern is his ability to continue correctly.

phrases.english: The one leading prayer should not answer “amen”
after the priests, because of possible confusion.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָעוֹבֵר לִפְנֵי הַתֵּיבָה לֹא יַעֲנֶה ״אָמֵן״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from replacing a leader after a mistake to preventing a mistake.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The prayer leader does not answer אָמֵן after the priests because he may become confused.

steps.title: A prayer leader who is the only priest does not lift his hands
steps.stepSummary: If the prayer leader is the only כהן, he normally does not perform נשיאת כפים.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there is no priest there except him, he should not lift his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה applies the same concern about confusion to a leader who is also the only priest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Performing נשיאת כפים could make it hard for him to resume the prayer. The next step gives a limited exception.

keyTerms.meaning: lift his hands for the priestly blessing

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אֵין שָׁם כֹּהֵן אֶלָּא הוּא —
phrases.english: And if there is no priest there except him—
he should not lift his hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אֵין שָׁם כֹּהֵן אֶלָּא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the concern about confusion from answering אָמֵן to performing נשיאת כפים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A leader who is the only כהן normally does not perform נשיאת כפים.

steps.title: An exception when he can resume confidently
steps.stepSummary: The leader may bless if he is confident he can return to the prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he is confident that he can lift his hands and return to his prayer, he is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה qualifies the previous restriction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The restriction was based on the risk of losing his place. When he is confident he can resume, that reason does not prevent him from blessing.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם הַבְטָחָתוֹ שֶׁהוּא נוֹשֵׂא אֶת כַּפָּיו,
phrases.english: But if he is confident that he can lift his hands,
and return to his prayer, he is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם הַבְטָחָתוֹ שֶׁהוּא נוֹשֵׂא אֶת כַּפָּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Makes an exception to the restriction in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He may perform נשיאת כפים if he is confident he can resume leading the תפילה.
steps.whatToRemember: The concern in these two rules is that the leader might lose his place; confidence that he can resume changes the נשיאת כפים case.

steps.title: Ordinarily, a person asked to lead should decline at first
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that neither immediate acceptance nor excessive refusal is appropriate.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: One asked to lead prayer should refuse. Not refusing is like food without salt; refusing too much is like food spoiled by salt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces a ברייתא about the normal situation in which someone is asked to lead prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sets up a contrast with the urgent replacement in the משנה. In an ordinary invitation, some reluctance is appropriate, but too much becomes inappropriate too.

phrases.english: Gemara: The Sages taught:
One asked to lead prayer should initially refuse.
And if he does not refuse—
he is like cooked food that has no salt.
And if he refuses too much—
he is like cooked food spoiled by salt.

steps.triggerLanguage: גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the question of refusing to lead, which arose in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under ordinary circumstances, a person asked to lead should show some initial reluctance, but not refuse excessively.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not overturn the משנה. An ordinary invitation allows initial refusal; replacing someone who has already made a mistake calls for an immediate response.

steps.title: A three-stage response to an invitation
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא spells out when to refuse, hesitate, and then accept.
steps.simpleTranslation: How should he act? The first time, refuse; the second, hesitate; the third, step forward and go down to lead.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא turns its warning about too little or too much refusal into a practical sequence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He declines the first request and shows hesitation at the second. At the third, he accepts and goes to lead.

keyTerms.meaning: stretches out his legs to step forward

phrases.english: How should he act?
The first time, he should refuse;
the second time, he should hesitate;
the third time, he steps forward and goes down to lead.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד הוּא עוֹשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the practical middle course between the two extremes in step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Refuse the first time, hesitate the second, and accept the third.
steps.whatToRemember: Ordinary invitation: refuse, hesitate, then accept. Emergency replacement after a mistake: do not refuse.

steps.title: Three things are good in small amounts
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that too much leaven, salt, or refusal is harmful, but a little is good.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: Three things are harmful in large amounts and good in small amounts: leaven, salt, and refusal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a ברייתא to the discussion of how much refusal is appropriate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous ברייתא described when to refuse and when to accept. This one gives the simple guiding idea: some refusal is appropriate, but too much is not.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: There are three things of which a large amount is harmful,
but a small amount is good; and these are they:
leaven, salt, and refusal.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שְׁלֹשָׁה רוּבָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a general rule of moderation to the earlier instructions about refusal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A small amount of refusal is fitting; excessive refusal is not.

steps.title: Where to resume after an error in each section of prayer
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא assigns a return point for errors in the first, middle, and last groups of ברכות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: If one erred in the first three ברכות, one returns to the beginning. In the middle ברכות, one returns to אַתָּה חוֹנֵן. In the last ברכות, one returns to עֲבוֹדָה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new discussion about where someone resumes the עמידה after an error.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא divides the ברכות into three groups. In his ruling, an error sends the person back to the start of the relevant group, not just to the particular ברכה where the error occurred.

keyTerms.meaning: the opening words of the first middle blessing
the blessing about the Temple service

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: טָעָה בְּשָׁלֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת —
phrases.english: Rav Huna said: If one erred in the first three blessings—
one returns to the beginning.
In the middle blessings—one returns to “You grace.”
In the last blessings—one returns to “Service.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: טָעָה בְּשָׁלֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's rule about where to resume after an error (step 5) and qualifies it by section of the תפילה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After an error, return to the beginning of the relevant group of ברכות.

steps.title: The middle blessings do not have a fixed order
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי disagrees with the required return point for the middle ברכות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב אסי said: The middle ברכות have no fixed order.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אסי gives a different rule for the middle ברכות. This sets up the disagreement that the next step will test.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא required a return to אַתָּה חוֹנֵן after an error in the middle section. רב אסי’s statement rejects treating that return point as mandatory.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage who gives the differing view

phrases.english: And Rav Asi said:
The middle blessings have no fixed order.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב אַסִּי אָמַר: אֶמְצָעִיּוֹת אֵין לָהֶן סֵדֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב הונא about how to handle an error in the middle ברכות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The middle ברכות have no fixed order, so one who erred in them need not go back to אַתָּה חוֹנֵן; he may say the missed ברכה where he realizes his error.

steps.title: A source says to return to the blessing where the error occurred
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת cites a source that names the mistaken ברכה itself as the return point, and the גמרא declares רב הונא refuted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת objected: From where does one resume? From the beginning of the ברכה in which this person erred. This refutes רב הונא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת challenges רב הונא with a source that gives a different return point, and frames it as a refutation of רב הונא. The next step answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא sent a person back to the beginning of a whole group of ברכות. The cited source instead says to begin with the particular ברכה where the error occurred; that direct difference drives the objection.

keyTerms.meaning: from the beginning of the blessing

steps.whatToRemember: The quoted source seems to say to restart the mistaken ברכה itself. The next step shows how רב הונא answers this apparent refutation.

phrases.aramaic: מֵתִיב רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: מֵהֵיכָן הוּא חוֹזֵר —
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet objected: From where does one resume—
from the beginning of the blessing in which this person erred.
This is a conclusive refutation of Rav Huna.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: מֵהֵיכָן הוּא חוֹזֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רב הונא’s ruling against a source that appears to contradict it; step 15 answers the challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא’s rule to return to the beginning of the group of ברכות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The cited source says to return to the beginning of the particular mistaken ברכה, rather than the beginning of its group.

steps.title: The middle blessings count as one unit
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא can answer רב ששת's challenge. All the middle ברכות together count as one ברכה, so "returning to the start of the ברכה" means going back to the start of the middle section.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא could say to you: all the middle ברכות are really one ברכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rescues רב הונא from רב ששת's challenge. It reads the source in a way that fits רב הונא's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת's source said a person who makes a mistake goes back to "the beginning of the ברכה." That sounded like it meant only the specific ברכה where he made the mistake. רב הונא answers that all the middle ברכות form one big ברכה, so "the beginning of the ברכה" means the start of the middle section. That is exactly what רב הונא said.

keyTerms.meaning: The middle ברכות of שמונה עשרה (the requests)
"He could say to you": the גמרא answering on someone's behalf

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the middle ברכות are literally one ברכה in every way. It only means that for this rule, about where to go back after a mistake, they are treated as one unit.

phrases.english: Rav Huna could say to you:
the middle blessings, all of them
are one blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge brought by רב ששת in step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a term in the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "The beginning of the ברכה" means the beginning of the specific ברכה where he made the mistake.
steps.terutzMaskana: "The beginning of the ברכה" means the beginning of the whole middle section, because the middle ברכות count as one.

steps.title: Personal requests belong only in the middle blessings
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that a person should ask for his own needs only in the middle ברכות, and never in the first three or the last three.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: a person should never ask for his needs in the first three ברכות or the last three. He should ask only in the middle ones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule about the three sections of שמונה עשרה. It tells us where personal requests may be added.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new topic, but it builds on the same division of the תפילה into three parts. Earlier steps used that division for fixing mistakes. Here it decides where a person may add his own requests.

keyTerms.meaning: The first three ברכות of שמונה עשרה
The last three ברכות of שמונה עשרה

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practical הלכה that you add your own requests in the middle ברכות, such as in שומע תפילה.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
a person should never request his needs
not in the first three,
and not in the last three,
but rather in the middle ones.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה לְעוֹלָם אַל יִשְׁאַל אָדָם צְרָכָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new rule about the same three sections of the תפילה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Personal requests may be added only in the middle ברכות.

steps.title: The servant comparison explains the three sections
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא compares the three sections of the תפילה to a servant: first he praises his master, then he asks for a gift, then he takes his leave after receiving it.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי חנינא said: in the first ברכות, a person is like a servant who arranges praise before his master. In the middle ברכות, he is like a servant asking his master for a gift. In the last ברכות, he is like a servant who already received the gift and is now leaving.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רב יהודה's rule with רבי חנינא's comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each section has its own job: praise, then asking, then thanks and goodbye. Asking for things during the praise or the goodbye does not fit what that section is for. That is why requests belong only in the middle.

keyTerms.meaning: A gift or reward (here, what one asks for)

phrases.english: As Rabbi Chanina said:
the first ones: he is like a servant
who arranges praise before his master.
the middle ones: he is like a servant
who requests a reward from his master.
the last ones: he is like a servant
who received a reward from his master,
and takes leave and goes on his way.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind רב יהודה's rule.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's rule that requests belong only in the middle ברכות
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חנינא's comparison of the תפילה to a servant before his master

steps.title: רבי אליעזר defends a very long prayer
steps.stepSummary: A student led the prayers and made them very long. רבי אליעזר defended him by pointing out that משה prayed for forty days and forty nights.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: once a student led the prayers in front of רבי אליעזר and made them extremely long. רבי אליעזר's students said, "How long-winded he is!" He answered them: "Is he making it longer than משה רבינו? About him it says, 'the forty days and the forty nights.'"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a story showing that a long prayer is acceptable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students thought making the prayer so long was a problem. רבי אליעזר showed from משה רבינו, who prayed for forty days, that a long prayer is not wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Went down before the ark, meaning he led the prayers

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
There was an incident with one student
who went down before the ark (to lead the prayers)
in the presence of Rabbi Eliezer,
and he was prolonging excessively.
His students said to him:
How long-winded this one is!
He said to them:
Is he prolonging more than Moses our teacher,
about whom it is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵת אַרְבָּעִים הַיּוֹם וְאֶת אַרְבָּעִים הַלַּיְלָה וְגוֹ׳״?!
phrases.english: "the forty days and the forty nights, etc."?!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן מַעֲשֶׂה בְּתַלְמִיד אֶחָד שֶׁיָּרַד לִפְנֵי הַתֵּיבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new topic about prayer: how long it should be.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A long prayer is legitimate, as shown by משה's forty days of prayer.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר defends a very short prayer
steps.stepSummary: Another student made the prayers very short. רבי אליעזר defended him too: משה's prayer for מרים was only five words long.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another time, a student led the prayers in front of רבי אליעזר and made them extremely short. His students said, "How brief he is!" He answered them: "Is he making it shorter than משה רבינו? It says, 'Please, God, heal her, please.'"
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells a second, opposite story to show that a short prayer is also acceptable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the complaint is that the prayer was too short. רבי אליעזר points to משה's tiny five-word prayer for מרים. Together, the two stories teach that both long and short prayers have a proper place.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is overly brief
"Please, God, heal her, please": משה's prayer for מרים

steps.whatToRemember: There is no single required length for a prayer. משה prayed both very long and very short, depending on what the moment called for.

phrases.english: Again there was an incident with one student
who went down before the ark (to lead the prayers)
in the presence of Rabbi Eliezer,
and he was abbreviating excessively.
His students said to him:
How brief this one is!
He said to them:
Is he abbreviating more than Moses our teacher,
as it is written:
"Please, God, heal her, please."

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוּב מַעֲשֶׂה בְּתַלְמִיד אֶחָד שֶׁיָּרַד לִפְנֵי הַתֵּיבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror-image story that completes the lesson of step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A short prayer is also legitimate, as shown by משה's five-word prayer for מרים.

steps.title: No need to say the name when praying for someone else
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that a person asking mercy for someone else does not need to say that person's name. He proves it from משה's prayer for מרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב said in the name of רב חסדא: Anyone who asks for mercy for another person does not need to mention that person's name. We see this from the verse "Please, God, heal her, please" (אל נא רפא נא לה), where משה did not mention מרים's name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stays with the פסוק it just quoted (משה's five-word prayer for מרים) and learns a new הלכה from it: when praying for someone else, you don't have to say their name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the previous step the verse showed that a short prayer is acceptable. Here the same verse teaches a second lesson. משה said "heal her" and never said "מרים", so mentioning the name is not required. The point is that the name is not necessary, not that saying it is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: One who asks for mercy, meaning someone who prays for help

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase "אין צריך" means "does not need to." It does NOT mean you are forbidden to say the name. Saying the name is allowed; it just isn't required.
steps.whyThisMatters: This connects to the common practice of davening for sick people. The גמרא here says that leaving out the name does not weaken the prayer.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ya'akov said that Rav Chisda said:
phrases.notes: Attribution line; it is merged into this step.

phrases.english: Anyone who requests mercy on behalf of his fellow
need not mention his name,
as it is stated: "Please, God, heal her, please,"
phrases.notes: The same verse as in Step 19.

phrases.english: and he did not mention Miriam's name.
phrases.notes: Aramaic explanation of how the verse proves the point.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same פסוק from Step 19 to learn a second, separate הלכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person praying for someone else does not need to mention that person's name.

steps.title: Where a person bows in the עמידה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a person bows at the beginning and end of the ברכה of אבות and the ברכה of הודאה. If he wants to bow at every ברכה, he is taught not to.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: These are the ברכות in which a person bows. In אבות (the first ברכה), at the beginning and at the end. In הודאה (the thanksgiving ברכה, מודים), at the beginning and at the end. If he wants to bow at the end and the beginning of every single ברכה, we teach him not to bow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a new rule about the עמידה: exactly where a person bows. Bowing is limited to two ברכות, at their beginnings and ends.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are four bowing points in total: the start and end of אבות, and the start and end of הודאה. A person who wants to add extra bows at other ברכות is stopped. Adding bows beyond what the חכמים set up is not treated as extra piety; it changes their arrangement.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught; this introduces a ברייתא
The first ברכה of the עמידה (the Patriarchs)
The thanksgiving ברכה (מודים), near the end of the עמידה
We teach him, meaning we instruct or correct him

steps.confusionAlert: Bowing more does not count as "extra credit" here. The ברייתא says we actively stop a person who adds bows.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practice of bowing at the beginning and end of אבות and of מודים, and only there.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
These are the blessings in which a person bows:
In "Patriarchs," at the beginning and the end.
In "Thanksgiving," at the beginning and the end.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם בָּא לָשׁוּחַ בְּסוֹף כׇּל בְּרָכָה וּבְרָכָה,
phrases.english: And if he comes to bow at the end of each and every blessing,
and at the beginning of each and every blessing,
they teach him not to bow.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵלּוּ בְּרָכוֹת שֶׁאָדָם שׁוֹחֶה בָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, bowing during the עמידה, while still discussing how the תפילה is structured.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bow only at the beginning and end of אבות and of הודאה. Someone who tries to bow at every ברכה is told not to.

steps.title: This bowing rule is for an ordinary person
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי, in the name of בר קפרא, says the bowing rule just taught applies to a הדיוט, an ordinary person. This sets up rules for people of higher rank.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן פזי said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי, who said it in the name of בר קפרא: An ordinary person (הדיוט) bows the way we said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the ברייתא's bowing rule to an ordinary person. This is a setup line: by saying "an ordinary person," it prepares for the next teaching about people of higher rank, who bow differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave one rule without saying who it applies to. בר קפרא now says it describes the regular person. Calling it the rule for a הדיוט signals that the גמרא is about to list people of higher status with different bowing rules.

keyTerms.meaning: An ordinary person, with no special rank or position
As we said, meaning according to the rule just stated

steps.confusionAlert: Here "הדיוט" just means a regular person, as opposed to someone with special rank. It is not an insult and does not mean an ignorant person.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said
phrases.notes: Attribution chain; it is merged into this step.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי מִשּׁוּם בַּר קַפָּרָא:
phrases.english: that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said in the name of bar Kappara:
An ordinary person, as we said.
phrases.notes: This is the first item in a list that continues on the next עמוד.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן פַּזִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי מִשּׁוּם בַּר קַפָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines who the ברייתא's bowing rule from Step 21 applies to, and prepares for a contrast with people of higher rank.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The bowing rule of the ברייתא (start and end of אבות and הודאה only) applies to an ordinary person.
